claims.text: An ML-enhanced multiscale framework trained on ab initio defective configurations will predict electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr within 10% error.
The claimed accuracy applies to both pristine HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The claimed accuracy applies over both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Statistically integrating defect-induced scattering will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy.
The framework will account for quantum effects at low temperature and thermally activated defect dynamics at high temperature.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen to HfNbTaTiZr introduces oxygen complexes, vacancy clusters, and local lattice distortions.
A diverse training set spanning defect microstructures and temperatures can capture defect-induced electron and phonon scattering effects on conductivity.
Quantum and defect-vibrational effects are significant in the 0–200 K regime.
Thermally activated defect dynamics prevail in the 300–1200 K regime.
Explicit vacancy clusters, interstitials, and oxygen-related defects in supercells provide a representation of the real imperfect crystal.
Defective configurations cause localized changes in electron-phonon coupling and scattering pathways.
Defects modify both electron and phonon transport.
An ML model can learn relationships between defect-induced scattering and resulting conductivity.
Representing defects will make the framework more faithful to real HfNbTaTiZr behavior than idealized analytical models.
Existing analytical and ab initio predictions based on perfect crystals fail to reproduce temperature-dependent conductivity in defective HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Existing predictions have errors greater than 10% relative to experimental HfNbTaTiZr conductivity data.
The framework is expected to be reliable only for bulk HfNbTaTiZr with zero or 1 wt.% oxygen within the studied temperature intervals.
A prediction differing by more than 10% from a held-out 300 K conductivity measurement of the 1 wt.% oxygen specimen falsifies the hypothesis.
